I don't think the heating from 200km/h wind is measurable. Once you get to 2-3000km/h (fast supersonic jets) the expansion from air friction heating is noticeable as an airframe design consideration. Low Earth orbit reentry speeds are typically 17,000km/h.

It's a common misconception that spacecraft heat up due to friction. It's actually because they're moving so fast the air gets compressed, and that's what makes it hot. That heat then gets transferred to the ship.

The reason moving air (from wind, a fan, or whatever) feels cold is because it's cooler than your body temperature. Air is a poor conductor of heat, so when it isn't moving, the air right next to your skin heats up, then stays there insulating you. When it's moving, new cooler air keeps replacing the air that your body heat has warmed up. If the air around you were warmer than your body temperature, then moving air would actually feel even warmer than still air.
Try standing in a 17,000 mph wind because that's the speed a spacecraft is traveling when it enters Earth's atmosphere. Your body would heat up as much.
